A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent.

Applies. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.
Applies. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

Applies. Berkeley landlords may not use rent-pricing software that relies on non-public competitor data (less than 90 days old) to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels, and vendors may not sell such software to Berkeley landlords. A tenant whose landlord uses such software can sue for an injunction, damages, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees.

Applies. If a Berkeley landlord charges an application or credit-report fee, it must give you, in the application or a separate disclosure before taking the fee, a Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and the maximum fee allowed under state law.
Applies. Your Berkeley landlord cannot charge you a non-refundable fee to renew your tenancy or to add, replace, or remove a roommate; lease terms saying otherwise are unenforceable.

Applies. If your landlord evicts you to take the property off the rental market under the Ellis Act, they must pay you relocation assistance. Starting January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

Applies. Tenants in fully or partially covered Berkeley units can only be evicted with just cause; for nonpayment, the landlord cannot evict unless you owe at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent for a comparable unit in the Oakland-Fremont area.

Applies. Most Berkeley rental units, including new construction, single-family homes and condos, are covered by Berkeley's just cause eviction protections, so a landlord needs a lawful reason to evict. Exempt units include Golden Duplexes, units where you share a kitchen or bath with a resident owner, certain owner-occupied ADU properties, university housing, and nonprofit cooperatives. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for an owner move-in, they must pay you relocation assistance. Starting January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you live in a fully covered Berkeley unit, your landlord's yearly increase is limited to the Annual General Adjustment set by the Rent Board, which can never exceed 5%. A landlord with unused (banked) prior adjustments may still raise rent more than 5% up to the lawful rent ceiling. (Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-12-31, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. For 2026, eligible Berkeley landlords may raise a covered unit's rent ceiling by no more than 1.0%, and not before January 1, 2026. The landlord must meet the qualifying conditions in Regulation 1148 and give the required notice. Tenants can contact the Rent Board at 510-981-7368 with questions. (Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-12-31, and the year built is not in the data.) Coverage cutoff taken from r-0054 (Berkeley Measure BB (Nov. 2024) amending Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Good Cause Ordinance), the same city's rent rule, because this record states none. Other records give a different cutoff: r-0056 1980-06-30.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you rent most units in a Berkeley multifamily building built before 1980, or a single-family home or rooming-house room whose tenancy began before 1996, your unit is under Berkeley rent control. Newer construction, most condos, and single-family homes with tenancies starting in 1996 or later are registered but not rent controlled. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-06-30, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. Berkeley landlords may not ask about, require disclosure of, or use your criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, rent or deposit amounts, or decisions to evict or add family members. If a landlord takes action against you based on criminal history (where an exemption allows it), they must give you written notice and a chance to respond, and you can file a complaint with the Rent Board. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your unit is fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, your landlord must pay you interest on your security deposit at the end of each year. If you move out before year-end, you are owed a prorated amount.

A0335.explanation: Applies. In California it is unlawful for a landlord or software vendor to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend or set prices or terms) as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce others into adopting its recommended price or terms. If you suspect coordinated algorithmic rent-setting, you can report it to the Attorney General or consult a lawyer about antitrust remedies.

Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. It is illegal for anyone using or distributing a shared pricing algorithm to coerce another person to adopt the price or commercial terms (such as availability or level of service) it recommends. This can cover pressure to adopt software-recommended rents.

Applies. A landlord may charge you at most $68.96 in 2026 to screen your application, must give you a receipt, an itemized cost list, a copy of any credit report, and a refund of any unused part of the fee. The landlord cannot charge a fee if no unit is available, and must refund the fee if you are not selected unless it uses a first-qualified-applicant policy and charges only applicants it considers.

Applies. A landlord cannot charge a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or soon. To charge a fee, the landlord must either consider applications first-come in writing-disclosed order, charging only when your application is actually considered, or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.

Applies. The landlord must give you a receipt itemizing the out-of-pocket costs and time spent screening you, delivered in person, by mail, or by email if you agree. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days of receiving it.

Covered, but superseded here: Just cause required to evict tenants in units covered by the Rent Ordinance (S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9(a)) governs this address. Once you have lawfully lived in your unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), your landlord can only end your tenancy for a just cause listed in the law and must state it in the written notice. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, or substantial remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your final month's rent; otherwise the notice is void.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).)

Covered, but superseded here: Annual allowable rent increase for rent-controlled units, March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 (S.F. Admin. Code § 37.3) governs this address. Within any 12-month period, your landlord may not raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, and may raise it in no more than two steps. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, ignoring discounts. If you have been overcharged, you can sue for the excess, and for up to three times the excess if the landlord acted willfully.

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources.
Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent.

Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

Applies. A California landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or give you different terms such as a higher deposit, because of how you pay rent, including a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department within one year or sue in court within two years. (10 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Since July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, whether or not the unit is furnished. Last month's rent counts toward the cap; first month's rent does not. Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent. (10 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. (10 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent.

Applies. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.
Applies. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

Applies. Landlords in San Francisco may not use, and vendors may not sell, software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents or manage occupancy. If you believe a landlord or vendor is violating this, you (or the City Attorney) can bring a civil lawsuit.

Applies. A landlord can only evict you from a unit covered by the SF Rent Ordinance for one of 17 listed just causes, and that cause must be the landlord's dominant motive. A lease simply expiring or the building being sold is not a just cause, and a landlord also needs just cause to remove housing services such as parking, storage, or laundry.

Applies. If you are served an Ellis Act eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27, you are owed $11,110.05 per tenant, up to $33,330.13 per unit. Each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant gets an additional $7,443.90.

Applies. If you are served an eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27 for owner or relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, you are owed $8,245 per tenant, up to $24,733 per unit. Each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant, or household with minor children, gets an additional $5,497.

Applies. If your San Francisco landlord serves an Ellis Act eviction notice between 3/1/2026 and 2/28/2027, you are owed $11,110.05 per tenant, up to $33,330.13 per unit. Each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant gets an additional $7,443.90.

Applies. If you live in a rent-controlled unit in San Francisco, your landlord's annual increase for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is limited to 1.6% of your base rent. For example, on a $2,000 base rent the increase is $32, for a new base rent of $2,032. (built 1968, before the 1979-06-13 cutoff.)

Applies. For a rent-controlled San Francisco unit, the annual increase your landlord can impose for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%. Check that any annual increase notice in this period does not exceed it. (built 1968, before the 1979-06-13 cutoff.) Coverage cutoff taken from r-0091 (S.F. Admin. Code § 37.3), the same city's rent rule, because this record states none.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are applying for affordable housing in San Francisco and have an arrest or conviction history, the Fair Chance Ordinance limits how that history can be used in the housing decision. You can contact the Human Rights Commission to file a complaint. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Unit must be affordable housing.)

A0336.explanation: Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. This Massachusetts bill would address algorithmic rent fixing in rental housing, but it is not law. It was reported favorably by the Joint Committee on Housing on 3/12/2026 and referred to House Ways and Means, so renters have no new rights under it yet.

Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. A Massachusetts bill would ban algorithmic rent setting, but it is not law. As of the latest action it was referred to the Senate Committee on Ways and Means, so it gives renters no rights yet.

Applies. In Massachusetts, a rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. If the landlord hired the broker, you as a tenant cannot be made to pay that fee.

Applies. At or before move-in, a landlord or the landlord's agent can only require you to pay first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. Since August 1, 2025, this also bars requiring you to pay the landlord's agent (such as the landlord's broker) anything beyond those items.

Applies. If you fall behind on rent under a written lease, your landlord must give you a written 14-day notice to quit before ending the lease. You can stop the eviction by paying all rent due, plus interest and court costs, by the day your answer is due in the eviction case. If the late rent was caused by a delayed government payment or voucher, the court must postpone the hearing at least 7 days so you can pay.

Applies. Massachusetts state law does not require a reason to end a tenancy at will, but the landlord must give written notice equal to the rent payment interval or 30 days, whichever is longer (three months if rent is paid less often). A notice ending your tenancy may also offer a new tenancy on different terms.

Applies. If your landlord gives you a written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, it must come with a state form listing any repayment agreements, rental assistance programs (such as RAFT), court rules, and eviction protections, and stating that the notice is not an eviction. A court cannot accept the landlord's nonpayment eviction filing without proof that this form was delivered to you.

Applies. Massachusetts cities and towns generally cannot enact, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no local rent cap to rely on. The only exception is a voluntary program for owners of 10 or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less, where the city pays owners the difference from its general funds.

Applies. A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or otherwise discriminate against you because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher, or because of that program's requirements. Ads may not state a preference against public assistance recipients.

Applies. Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit larger than one month's rent, must put it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and must give you a signed statement of the apartment's condition. If the state housing office issues regulations, a landlord may offer an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, and deposit plus fees can never exceed one month's rent in total.

Applies. Your landlord must return your security deposit, minus only unpaid rent/water charges, allowed tax escalation, or documented damage beyond normal wear and tear, within 30 days after you move out, and must pay you yearly interest on it. If the landlord fails to return it on time, you can sue for three times the amount owed plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Applies. Landlords and rental agents in Cambridge may not refuse to rent to you, or set different terms, because of your source of income, including a Section 8 voucher or public benefits. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Cambridge Human Rights Commission (617-349-4396). (468 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

A0337.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site.

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (at least 5 units (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. (Unknown: buildings newer than 30 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.) Flag for review: may preempt Newark Mun. Code § 19:2-3 (Ord. 6 PSF-A(S), 9-5-17).

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because of your lawful source of income or rent payment, such as a Section 8 voucher. You may file a free complaint with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or sue in Superior Court within two years. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In Newark rent-controlled units, rent may not rise more than the allowed percentage in any 12-month period, and never more than 4%, even if tenants or owners change. No increase is allowed if the building is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered the unit, so check the registration with the Office of Rent Control. Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

Applies. It is illegal for anyone using or distributing a shared pricing algorithm to coerce another person to adopt the price or commercial terms (such as availability or level of service) it recommends. This can cover pressure to adopt software-recommended rents.

Applies. A landlord may charge you at most $68.96 in 2026 to screen your application, must give you a receipt, an itemized cost list, a copy of any credit report, and a refund of any unused part of the fee. The landlord cannot charge a fee if no unit is available, and must refund the fee if you are not selected unless it uses a first-qualified-applicant policy and charges only applicants it considers.

Applies. A landlord cannot charge a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or soon. To charge a fee, the landlord must either consider applications first-come in writing-disclosed order, charging only when your application is actually considered, or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.

Applies. The landlord must give you a receipt itemizing the out-of-pocket costs and time spent screening you, delivered in person, by mail, or by email if you agree. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days of receiving it.

Covered, but superseded here: RSO legal reasons for eviction and relocation assistance (LAMC § 151.09 (§ 151.09.C.9; § 165.05.B.5)) governs this address. Once you have lawfully lived in your unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), your landlord can only end your tenancy for a just cause listed in the law and must state it in the written notice. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, or substantial remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your final month's rent; otherwise the notice is void.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).)

Covered, but superseded here: Rent Stabilization Ordinance coverage (pre-October 1978 certificate of occupancy) (Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (L.A. Mun. Code ch. XV)) governs this address. Within any 12-month period, your landlord may not raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, and may raise it in no more than two steps. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, ignoring discounts. If you have been overcharged, you can sue for the excess, and for up to three times the excess if the landlord acted willfully.

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources.
Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent.

Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

Applies. A California landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or give you different terms such as a higher deposit, because of how you pay rent, including a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department within one year or sue in court within two years. (50 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Since July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, whether or not the unit is furnished. Last month's rent counts toward the cap; first month's rent does not. Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent. (50 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. (50 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent.

Applies. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.
Applies. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

Applies. In an RSO unit, your landlord can evict only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, lease violations, nuisance, or illegal use. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a resident manager, demolition, a government order, or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict, give 30- or 60-day notice (sometimes 120 days), and pay relocation assistance. All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days. (built 1959, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (50 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason once you have lived there six months or your original lease has expired. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in or demolition, the landlord must pay relocation assistance.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. If your household is lower income, you get the higher RPO or state amounts, up to $115,480 for extremely low income households under the City's standardized option. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether a non-RSO unit is a Protected Unit (affordability covenant, occupancy by lower-income households within 5 years, or Ellis withdrawal within 10 years); Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower) for enhanced payments.)

Applies. Your Los Angeles unit is covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance if its certificate of occupancy was first issued before October 1, 1978. Check your building's certificate of occupancy date to know whether RSO protections apply. (built 1959, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

Applies. If your LA unit was first built on or before October 1, 1978, your landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the city's published allowable percentage. Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or a 10% increase for an added dependent. Increases beyond this, such as for capital improvements, need LAHD approval. (built 1959, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. Starting February 2, 2026, a landlord of an RSO unit cannot add any extra percentage rent increase for utilities on top of the annual allowable increase. (built 1959, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.) Coverage cutoff taken from r-0077 (Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LAMC Chapter XV; replacement units LAMC § 151.28)), the same city's rent rule, because this record states none. Other records give a different cutoff: r-0076 1978-09-30.

Applies. If you rent an RSO unit in Los Angeles (certificate of occupancy first issued before October 1, 1978) and your landlord has held your deposit for at least a year, the landlord must pay you interest (3.03% for 2026, or the actual interest earned with a bank statement), as a direct payment or rent credit, and any unpaid interest when you move out. If unpaid, you can sue, including in Small Claims Court; the city will not investigate. (built 1959, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

(6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your landlord ends your tenancy for a no-fault reason, they must pay you two months of your current rent (three months if you are a senior aged 62 or older, or disabled), regardless of your income or length of tenancy. The landlord may instead waive the same amount of rent, and must pay a direct payment within 15 days of the notice. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A San Diego landlord may not refuse to rent or renew, end a tenancy, falsely say a unit is unavailable, or advertise a preference based on your source of income, which includes Section 8 and other rental, deposit, or homeless assistance. Any income standard must count all of your income, including assistance, plus the combined income of co-tenants and cosigners.

A0342.explanation: Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. This Massachusetts bill would address algorithmic rent fixing in rental housing, but it is not law. It was reported favorably by the Joint Committee on Housing on 3/12/2026 and referred to House Ways and Means, so renters have no new rights under it yet.

Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. A Massachusetts bill would ban algorithmic rent setting, but it is not law. As of the latest action it was referred to the Senate Committee on Ways and Means, so it gives renters no rights yet.

Applies. In Massachusetts, a rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. If the landlord hired the broker, you as a tenant cannot be made to pay that fee.

Applies. At or before move-in, a landlord or the landlord's agent can only require you to pay first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. Since August 1, 2025, this also bars requiring you to pay the landlord's agent (such as the landlord's broker) anything beyond those items.

Applies. If you fall behind on rent under a written lease, your landlord must give you a written 14-day notice to quit before ending the lease. You can stop the eviction by paying all rent due, plus interest and court costs, by the day your answer is due in the eviction case. If the late rent was caused by a delayed government payment or voucher, the court must postpone the hearing at least 7 days so you can pay.

Applies. Massachusetts state law does not require a reason to end a tenancy at will, but the landlord must give written notice equal to the rent payment interval or 30 days, whichever is longer (three months if rent is paid less often). A notice ending your tenancy may also offer a new tenancy on different terms.

Applies. If your landlord gives you a written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, it must come with a state form listing any repayment agreements, rental assistance programs (such as RAFT), court rules, and eviction protections, and stating that the notice is not an eviction. A court cannot accept the landlord's nonpayment eviction filing without proof that this form was delivered to you.

Applies. Massachusetts cities and towns generally cannot enact, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no local rent cap to rely on. The only exception is a voluntary program for owners of 10 or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less, where the city pays owners the difference from its general funds.

Applies. A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or otherwise discriminate against you because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher, or because of that program's requirements. Ads may not state a preference against public assistance recipients.

Applies. Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit larger than one month's rent, must put it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and must give you a signed statement of the apartment's condition. If the state housing office issues regulations, a landlord may offer an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, and deposit plus fees can never exceed one month's rent in total.

Applies. Your landlord must return your security deposit, minus only unpaid rent/water charges, allowed tax escalation, or documented damage beyond normal wear and tear, within 30 days after you move out, and must pay you yearly interest on it. If the landlord fails to return it on time, you can sue for three times the amount owed plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Applies. Landlords and rental agents in Cambridge may not refuse to rent to you, or set different terms, because of your source of income, including a Section 8 voucher or public benefits. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Cambridge Human Rights Commission (617-349-4396). (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

A0343.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site.

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (at least 5 units (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. (Unknown: buildings newer than 30 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.) Flag for review: may preempt Newark Mun. Code § 19:2-3 (Ord. 6 PSF-A(S), 9-5-17).

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because of your lawful source of income or rent payment, such as a Section 8 voucher. You may file a free complaint with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or sue in Superior Court within two years. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In Newark rent-controlled units, rent may not rise more than the allowed percentage in any 12-month period, and never more than 4%, even if tenants or owners change. No increase is allowed if the building is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered the unit, so check the registration with the Office of Rent Control. Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

Applies. If you rent in a Jersey City building with 5 or more units, your rent may be regulated under the city's Rent Control Ordinance. Covered, but superseded here: RSO legal reasons for eviction and relocation assistance (LAMC § 151.09 (§ 151.09.C.9; § 165.05.B.5)) governs this address. Once you have lawfully lived in your unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), your landlord can only end your tenancy for a just cause listed in the law and must state it in the written notice. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, or substantial remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your final month's rent; otherwise the notice is void.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Code § 7260 et seq. Covered, but superseded here: Rent Stabilization Ordinance coverage (pre-October 1978 certificate of occupancy) (Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (L.A. Mun. Code ch. XV)) governs this address. Within any 12-month period, your landlord may not raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, and may raise it in no more than two steps. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, ignoring discounts. If you have been overcharged, you can sue for the excess, and for up to three times the excess if the landlord acted willfully.

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources.
Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent.

Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

Applies. A California landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or give you different terms such as a higher deposit, because of how you pay rent, including a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department within one year or sue in court within two years. (5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Since July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, whether or not the unit is furnished. Last month's rent counts toward the cap; first month's rent does not. Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent. (5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. (5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent.

Applies. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.
Applies. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

Applies. In an RSO unit, your landlord can evict only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, lease violations, nuisance, or illegal use. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a resident manager, demolition, a government order, or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict, give 30- or 60-day notice (sometimes 120 days), and pay relocation assistance. All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days. (built 1921, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason once you have lived there six months or your original lease has expired. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in or demolition, the landlord must pay relocation assistance.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. If your household is lower income, you get the higher RPO or state amounts, up to $115,480 for extremely low income households under the City's standardized option. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether a non-RSO unit is a Protected Unit (affordability covenant, occupancy by lower-income households within 5 years, or Ellis withdrawal within 10 years); Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower) for enhanced payments.)

Applies. Your Los Angeles unit is covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance if its certificate of occupancy was first issued before October 1, 1978. Check your building's certificate of occupancy date to know whether RSO protections apply. (built 1921, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

Applies. If your LA unit was first built on or before October 1, 1978, your landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the city's published allowable percentage. Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or a 10% increase for an added dependent. Increases beyond this, such as for capital improvements, need LAHD approval. (built 1921, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. Starting February 2, 2026, a landlord of an RSO unit cannot add any extra percentage rent increase for utilities on top of the annual allowable increase. (built 1921, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.) Coverage cutoff taken from r-0077 (Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LAMC Chapter XV; replacement units LAMC § 151.28)), the same city's rent rule, because this record states none. Applies. If you rent an RSO unit in Los Angeles (certificate of occupancy first issued before October 1, 1978) and your landlord has held your deposit for at least a year, the landlord must pay you interest (3.03% for 2026, or the actual interest earned with a bank statement), as a direct payment or rent credit, and any unpaid interest when you move out. If unpaid, you can sue, including in Small Claims Court; the city will not investigate. (built 1921, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

A0348.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site. Flag for review: may preempt Hoboken Code § 158-2 (ordinance adopted Jul 9, 2025; body heading reads § 154-8).

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (7 units (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. (Unknown: buildings newer than 30 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.) Flag for review: may preempt Hoboken Code § 155-31 (§§ 155-32, 155-34), Hoboken Code § 155-5 (Ord. No. C329, as amended by Ord. No. B-532), Hoboken Mun. Code ch. 155.

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because of your lawful source of income or rent payment, such as a Section 8 voucher. You may file a free complaint with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or sue in Superior Court within two years. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Hoboken landlords may not use software, algorithms or data-sharing platforms that collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information to coordinate, recommend or set rents, lease terms or occupancy levels. If you believe a landlord did this, you or the Division of Housing can bring the violation to the Hoboken Municipal Court. Flag for review: possible conflict with Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination (N.J.S.A. 56:9-20 to 56:9-26 (P.L. 2026, c.43; A3497 ACS 1R)).

Applies. When a tenant voluntarily leaves a registered rent-controlled unit, the landlord may raise the new tenant's first rent by at most 25% over the prior rent, and only once in any three-year period. Later increases are again controlled. Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

Applies. In a rent-controlled Hoboken unit, your landlord can raise rent only when your lease ends, once in any 12 months, by no more than 5% or the CPI change, whichever is less. The landlord must give 30 days' written notice with reasons and a certificate of substantial code compliance; increases above the legal amount are void and must be refunded, subject to a two-year limit. Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

Applies. Most Hoboken rental units, including many condos, are under rent control, and landlords must register them with the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Office by June 30 each year. A landlord who fails to register or to give proof of rent received can be denied a rent increase, so a tenant can check registration status and appeal through that office. Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

A0349.explanation: Applies. In California it is unlawful for a landlord or software vendor to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend or set prices or terms) as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce others into adopting its recommended price or terms. If you suspect coordinated algorithmic rent-setting, you can report it to the Attorney General or consult a lawyer about antitrust remedies.

Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. It is illegal for anyone using or distributing a shared pricing algorithm to coerce another person to adopt the price or commercial terms (such as availability or level of service) it recommends. This can cover pressure to adopt software-recommended rents.

Applies. A landlord may charge you at most $68.96 in 2026 to screen your application, must give you a receipt, an itemized cost list, a copy of any credit report, and a refund of any unused part of the fee. The landlord cannot charge a fee if no unit is available, and must refund the fee if you are not selected unless it uses a first-qualified-applicant policy and charges only applicants it considers.

Applies. A landlord cannot charge a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or soon. To charge a fee, the landlord must either consider applications first-come in writing-disclosed order, charging only when your application is actually considered, or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.

Applies. The landlord must give you a receipt itemizing the out-of-pocket costs and time spent screening you, delivered in person, by mail, or by email if you agree. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days of receiving it.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Once you have lawfully lived in your unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), your landlord can only end your tenancy for a just cause listed in the law and must state it in the written notice. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, or substantial remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your final month's rent; otherwise the notice is void. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Within any 12-month period, your landlord may not raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, and may raise it in no more than two steps. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, ignoring discounts. If you have been overcharged, you can sue for the excess, and for up to three times the excess if the landlord acted willfully. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources.
Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent.

Applies. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

Applies. A California landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or give you different terms such as a higher deposit, because of how you pay rent, including a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department within one year or sue in court within two years. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Since July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, whether or not the unit is furnished. Last month's rent counts toward the cap; first month's rent does not. Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent.

Applies. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.
Applies. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

Applies. Berkeley landlords may not use rent-pricing software that relies on non-public competitor data (less than 90 days old) to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels, and vendors may not sell such software to Berkeley landlords. A tenant whose landlord uses such software can sue for an injunction, damages, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees.

Applies. If a Berkeley landlord charges an application or credit-report fee, it must give you, in the application or a separate disclosure before taking the fee, a Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and the maximum fee allowed under state law.
Applies. Your Berkeley landlord cannot charge you a non-refundable fee to renew your tenancy or to add, replace, or remove a roommate; lease terms saying otherwise are unenforceable.

Applies. If your landlord evicts you to take the property off the rental market under the Ellis Act, they must pay you relocation assistance. Starting January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

Applies. Tenants in fully or partially covered Berkeley units can only be evicted with just cause; for nonpayment, the landlord cannot evict unless you owe at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent for a comparable unit in the Oakland-Fremont area.

Applies. Most Berkeley rental units, including new construction, single-family homes and condos, are covered by Berkeley's just cause eviction protections, so a landlord needs a lawful reason to evict. Exempt units include Golden Duplexes, units where you share a kitchen or bath with a resident owner, certain owner-occupied ADU properties, university housing, and nonprofit cooperatives. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for an owner move-in, they must pay you relocation assistance. Starting January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you live in a fully covered Berkeley unit, your landlord's yearly increase is limited to the Annual General Adjustment set by the Rent Board, which can never exceed 5%. A landlord with unused (banked) prior adjustments may still raise rent more than 5% up to the lawful rent ceiling. (Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-12-31, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. For 2026, eligible Berkeley landlords may raise a covered unit's rent ceiling by no more than 1.0%, and not before January 1, 2026. The landlord must meet the qualifying conditions in Regulation 1148 and give the required notice. Tenants can contact the Rent Board at 510-981-7368 with questions. (Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-12-31, and the year built is not in the data.) Coverage cutoff taken from r-0054 (Berkeley Measure BB (Nov. 2024) amending Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Good Cause Ordinance), the same city's rent rule, because this record states none. Other records give a different cutoff: r-0056 1980-06-30.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you rent most units in a Berkeley multifamily building built before 1980, or a single-family home or rooming-house room whose tenancy began before 1996, your unit is under Berkeley rent control. Newer construction, most condos, and single-family homes with tenancies starting in 1996 or later are registered but not rent controlled. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: covers buildings with certificate of occupancy on or before 1980-06-30, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. Berkeley landlords may not ask about, require disclosure of, or use your criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, rent or deposit amounts, or decisions to evict or add family members. If a landlord takes action against you based on criminal history (where an exemption allows it), they must give you written notice and a chance to respond, and you can file a complaint with the Rent Board. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your unit is fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, your landlord must pay you interest on your security deposit at the end of each year. If you move out before year-end, you are owed a prorated amount.

A0350.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site. Flag for review: may preempt Jersey City Code § 218-12 (Ord. 25-057).

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (6 units (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

Applies. If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. (built 1900, older than the 30-year new-construction exemption.) Flag for review: may preempt Jersey City Mun. Code ch. 260.

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because of your lawful source of income or rent payment, such as a Section 8 voucher. You may file a free complaint with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or sue in Superior Court within two years. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Jersey City landlords and their agents may not pay for or subscribe to services that collect competitors' rent, occupancy or lease data and use software to recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy levels, and such service providers may not facilitate agreements among landlords not to compete. If you have evidence your landlord uses such a service, you can report it to the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations or sue for injuries. Flag for review: possible conflict with Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination (N.J.S.A. 56:9-20 to 56:9-26 (P.L. 2026, c.43; A3497 ACS 1R)).

Applies. If you rent in a Jersey City building with 5 or more units, your rent may be regulated under the city's Rent Control Ordinance. You can ask the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations about your building's status through SeeClickFix or file an Illegal Rent Petition if you think your rent is illegal. (6 units (rule covers 5+).) Flag for review: possible conflict with Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)).

Applies. A landlord can only evict you from a unit covered by the SF Rent Ordinance for one of 17 listed just causes, and that cause must be the landlord's dominant motive. Applies. If you are served an Ellis Act eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27, you are owed $11,110.05 per tenant, up to $33,330.13 per unit. Each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant gets an additional $7,443.90.

Applies. If you are served an eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27 for owner or relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, you are owed $8,245 per tenant, up to $24,733 per unit. Each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant, or household with minor children, gets an additional $5,497.

Applies. If you live in a rent-controlled unit in San Francisco, your landlord's annual increase for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is limited to 1.6% of your base rent. Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (at least 5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)
